summary: Describes how to use TLS to secure NETCONF, the protocol for installing, changing and deleting the configuration of network devices. It was replaced by RFC 7589.

plainLanguage.summary: Managing network equipment remotely needs a private tunnel. This note says how to use the web-style lock, TLS, to keep those management messages safe. It was later replaced by RFC 7589.

questions: how to run netconf over tls
what port does netconf use over tls
subtitle: How to use TLS encryption to secure remote network device management.

tldr.problem: Network devices need a secure way for remote management software to configure them reliably and safely.
tldr.mechanism: NETCONF over TLS uses the TLS encryption protocol to secure NETCONF configuration messages, with certificate-based authentication on both sides.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can securely install, change and delete device configurations remotely, and it was later superseded by RFC 7589.

today: RFC 5539 defined NETCONF over TLS as a Proposed Standard in May 2009. It was later superseded by RFC 7589, which updated the specification.

sections.title: Introduction and Motivation
sections.content:
The Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF) is designed to help system administrators install, change and delete the configuration of network devices remotely. NETCONF requires a persistent, reliable connection and depends on the transport layer for security: the NETCONF protocol itself does not encrypt or authenticate messages.

This RFC explains how to use Transport Layer Security (TLS), the same encryption protocol that secures web browsers, to protect NETCONF exchanges. The approach uses TLS to provide encryption, mutual authentication with certificates, and reliable key negotiation.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF is a tool for managing network equipment from the Internet. This document says to wrap those management messages in TLS, the same lock that protects bank websites, so nobody can spy on or change the commands.

sections.title: Establishing and Closing Connections
sections.content:
A NETCONF client (the management station) acts as a TLS client and initiates a TLS connection to a NETCONF server (the network device) on TCP port 6513. After the TLS handshake completes, the client and server exchange NETCONF messages as XML documents: the client sends <rpc> elements and the server replies with <rpc-reply> elements.

Both sides can also use the TLS connection for NETCONF event notifications. After each XML document, both sides must send the delimiter sequence ]]>]]> to mark the end of the message, since this marks where one message stops and another begins. If the delimiter appears in the actual data, implementations must prevent it from being sent as part of a NETCONF message.

When the client has no more messages to send, it must close the connection gracefully by sending a TLS close_notify alert before shutting down the underlying TCP connection.
sections.plainLanguage: One side dials up to the other on port 6513 using TLS. Then they trade messages, each marked with ]]>]]> so they know where one stops and the next starts. When done, they politely hang up.

sections.title: Server and Client Identity Verification
sections.content:
During the TLS handshake, the client MUST check that the server's certificate matches the server's hostname or the hostname specified in the TLS server name extension. The client should verify the certificate binding using the X.509 algorithm defined in RFC 5280, checking that the public key in the certificate corresponds to the identity being verified. The certificate's Subject Alternative Name (dNSName) takes precedence if present. Wildcard certificates are allowed; for example, *.example.com matches a.example.com and foo.example.com.

The server MUST verify the client's certificate using its own policy to ensure the incoming request is legitimate before sharing any configuration or state data. The RFC notes that TLS does not support third-party authentication with external systems like RADIUS servers, so if that is needed, SSH or BEEP transport should be used instead.
sections.plainLanguage: The client checks that the server's name on its ID card matches the server it dialed. The server checks the client's ID card to make sure it is someone allowed to make changes. If anyone's ID looks wrong, the connection stops.

sections.title: Security and Implementation Issues
sections.content:
Implementations MUST support TLS 1.2 and are required to support the TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA cipher suite as a baseline. Servers MUST support certificate-based client authentication.

A critical risk is that the delimiter sequence ]]>]]> might appear inside NETCONF message data. If the delimiter is found in a message being sent, robust implementations should warn the user. If found on receipt, implementations MUST silently discard the message and stop the NETCONF session to prevent message corruption or spoofing.

An attacker might deliberately inject the delimiter into messages to cause a denial-of-service attack. Applications and NETCONF libraries must ensure this character sequence never appears in NETCONF messages.
sections.plainLanguage: Use a strong modern version of TLS and check both sides' ID cards. Watch out for someone sneaking the message-ending code into the data itself to break the conversation or trick the other side.

sections.title: Port Assignment
sections.content: IANA assigned TCP port 6513 as the default port for NETCONF over TLS. This port is registered as netconf-tls in the Registered Port Numbers range.
sections.plainLanguage: The standard door for this service is port 6513, registered with the Internet number authorities.
